01.note: Rav Avya the Elder put a hard question to Rabba bar Rav Huna: according to Rabbi Yishmael, does a sealed thigh bone of a carcass, which cannot make a person impure by touch, make him impure when he carries it? Instead of answering, Rabba bar Rav Huna said, "Look, a raven flies," to change the subject. His son Rava protested that this was the same Rav Avya his father always praised as a great man. Rabba bar Rav Huna explained that he was exhausted that day, quoting the Song of Songs, and the question needed careful reasoning he could not give on the spot.
01.why: The Gemara has just explained Rabbi Akiva's rule that what does not make impure by touch does not make impure by carrying; the unanswered question tests whether Rabbi Yishmael holds the same rule.

people.name: Rav Avya the Elder
people.about: A Sage of Pumbedita who asks the question; praised by Rabba bar Rav Huna as a great man

people.name: Rabba bar Rav Huna
people.about: The Sage who is asked and dodges the question because he is tired

people.name: Rava
people.about: Son of Rabba bar Rav Huna, who challenges his father's treatment of the guest

terms.meaning: The standard minimum amount, about the size of an olive, that a piece of a carcass must reach to transmit ritual impurity.
In Jewish law some impure things make a person ritually impure not only by touching them but also by lifting or carrying them, even without direct contact.

02.note: Rav Huna bar Torta told how he once went to the city of Va'ad and saw the locals placing a snake wrapped around a great lizard to breed them. After a time an arvad, a deadly biting snake, came out from between them. When he came before Rabbi Shimon the Righteous, Rabbi Shimon told him that God had said: they produced a creature I did not create in My world, so I will bring upon them a creature I did not create in My world.
02.why: The Gemara, returning to its survey of creatures and their kinds, follows the story by asking how a snake and a lizard with different gestation periods could breed at all; Rav answers that it was a miraculous calamity to punish the wicked.

people.name: Rav Huna bar Torta
people.about: The Sage who tells what he saw in Va'ad

people.name: Rabbi Shimon the Righteous
people.about: The Sage who explains the meaning of the event to Rav Huna bar Torta

people.name: The Holy One, Blessed be He
people.about: God, whose words Rabbi Shimon quotes, promising a creature-for-creature punishment

terms.meaning: A kind of snake that bites and kills people, here said to have come from crossbreeding a snake with a lizard.

03.note: Rabbi Tavla's host, a priest, was short of money. Rabbi Tavla advised him to go into partnership with Israelite butchers, who would take him in for free because a partnership with a priest exempts them from giving the priestly gifts. Rav Nahman nonetheless obligated the butcher to give the gifts and threatened to "remove Rabbi Tavla from your ear." Rabbi Tavla asked why; Rav Nahman cited a teaching that a priest who becomes a butcher is exempt for two or three weeks and then obligated. When Rabbi Tavla asked for at least those weeks, Rav Nahman said the exemption applies only to one who has not yet set up a shop, and this man already had.
03.why: The mishna exempts an animal owned jointly by an Israelite and a priest from the priestly gifts, and the Gemara has just said the gifts are claimed from the butcher; the story shows a Sage refusing to let that exemption be used as a business scheme.

people.name: Rabbi Tavla
people.about: A Sage whose host was a priest; he advises the partnership and later questions Rav Nahman's ruling

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: The judge who obligates the butcher to give the gifts despite the partnership

people.name: Rabbi Aha bar Hanina
people.about: A Sage who brought from the south the teaching Rav Nahman relies on

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
people.about: Sage who, with the elders of the south, said a priest-butcher is exempt only for his first weeks

terms.meaning: The foreleg, jaw and maw of a slaughtered animal, which the Torah says must be given to a priest (Deuteronomy 18:3).
A kohen, a descendant of Aaron, entitled to receive the priestly gifts.

04.note: Abaye, a priest, describes how his practice changed step by step. At first he would grab the priestly gifts, thinking this showed love for the commandment. When he learned the verse says the owner "shall give," he stopped grabbing and instead asked, "Give me." When he heard that the sons of Samuel sinned by asking for their portion, he stopped asking and only took what was offered. When he heard that the modest priests hold back while the gluttons take, he stopped taking at all, except on the eve of Yom Kippur, so that his standing as a priest would stay known.
04.why: Rav Yosef has just asked whether a priest who seizes his gifts honors or scorns the commandment, and Rava answered from the verse that he scorns it; Abaye's account shows that answer lived out, and the Gemara then asks why he did not prove his priesthood by giving the Priestly Benediction.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: A Sage who was a priest, telling how he came to stop taking the priestly gifts

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: Sage quoted in a teaching that the sons of Samuel sinned by asking for their portion

people.name: sons of Samuel
people.about: Levites who, the teaching says, sinned by demanding their portion out loud

terms.meaning: A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core collection of Jewish law.
Loaves displayed in the Temple each week and then divided among the priests to eat.
The day before the Day of Atonement, when it is a commandment to eat, so many animals were slaughtered and gifts were plentiful.

05.note: Rava and Rav Safra visited the house of Mar Yohana, who served them a choice calf. Rava asked Mar Yohana's attendant, a priest who normally received the priestly gifts, to grant them the gifts because he wanted to eat tongue with mustard. The attendant did; Rava ate and Rav Safra did not. Afterwards a verse from Proverbs was read to Rav Safra in a dream as a rebuke. He asked Rav Yosef whether it was because he had gone against Rav Yosef's ruling; Rav Yosef said no: his ruling covered only a priest giving freely to a needy scholar, not an attendant pressured into giving to a host's guest who could afford his own meat.
05.why: Rav Yosef has just ruled that a priest may assign his gifts to a poor Torah scholar; this incident marks the limits of that ruling, and the Gemara goes on to say the dream's rebuke was really meant for Rava.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage who asks for the priestly gifts and eats them

people.name: Rav Safra
people.about: Rava's companion, who does not eat and receives a rebuking verse in a dream

people.name: Mar Yohana
people.about: Their host, son of Rav Hana bar Adda (or, some say, of Rav Hana bar Bizna)

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: The Sage whose ruling is in question and who explains its limits to Rav Safra

terms.meaning: The foreleg, jaw (with the tongue) and maw of a slaughtered animal, which must be given to a priest.
A calf considered especially choice and tender, served to honored guests.

06.note: Rav Kahana said he had seen the pigeons named for King Herod standing in sixteen rows, each a mil wide, calling out "My master, my master." One of them did not say it. Another said to it, "Blind one, say 'My master, my master.'" It answered, "Blind one, say 'My master, my slave'" - since Herod was not a king but a slave. They took that pigeon and slaughtered it. Rav Ashi reported that Rabbi Hanina said of this "words"; the Gemara will not have him dismissing Rav Kahana's report and reads it as "through words" of witchcraft.
06.why: The mishna mentions domesticated pigeons, and the Gemara has just recorded that one reading of their name ties them to King Herod, who bred them; Rav Kahana's tale follows from that name.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: The Sage who says he saw the pigeons himself

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: Sage who reports Rabbi Hanina's comment on the story

people.name: Rabbi Hanina
people.about: Sage whose one-word comment the Gemara interprets

terms.meaning: A measure of distance used in the Talmud, roughly a kilometer.
King of Judea; the text says one name for these pigeons comes from him, as he bred them, and the pigeon calls him a slave rather than a king.

07.note: A certain man clipped a mother bird's wing, sent her away, and then caught her again. Rav Yehuda had him flogged and told him: go let her wings grow back, and then send her away.
07.why: Rav Yehuda has just taught that the mother bird must be sent far enough that she cannot be caught at once; the Gemara then asks whose view he followed, since flogging and sending her away seem to belong to different opinions, and answers that the lashes were rabbinic ones for defiance.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: The Sage who flogs the man and orders him to send the bird away properly

terms.meaning: The Torah commandment (Deuteronomy 22:6-7) that one who finds a nest must send away the mother before taking the eggs or chicks.
Whipped as a court punishment for breaking a commandment.

08.note: A man came to Rava asking whether the teima, a kosher bird, falls under the commandment of sending away the mother. Rava wondered aloud whether the man did not know that every kosher bird does. Pressed, the man said his doubt was about a nest with only a single egg, and Rava told him the mishna already rules that even one egg or one chick requires sending away the mother. The man sent the bird away, and Rava then surrounded her with nets and caught her. The Gemara asks whether Rava should have feared people would suspect his motive, and answers that he caught her in an unusual way.
08.why: The Gemara is discussing how a mother bird is to be sent away and whether she may be caught again afterwards; this incident shows that once she is properly sent off, catching her later is allowed.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who answers the man's question and then catches the released bird

terms.meaning: The name of a kosher bird the man was unsure about.
The early collection of Jewish law that the Gemara discusses; Rava quotes its ruling about a single egg.
The Torah commandment that one who finds a nest must send away the mother before taking the eggs or chicks.

09.note: Levi bar Simon transferred to Rav Yehuda the produce of his dovecote, its chicks and eggs. Rav Yehuda came to Shmuel, who told him: go bang on the nest so the birds rise up, and acquire them. The Gemara asks why this was needed and answers that this was a new brood Levi bar Simon himself did not yet own; banging on the nest would make the mothers fly up so that Levi bar Simon acquired the young, and he could then transfer them to Rav Yehuda by the formal handing over of a cloth.
09.why: The Gemara has just ruled that a courtyard cannot acquire eggs for its owner while the mother sits on them; this case of dovecote pigeons applies that ruling.

people.name: Levi bar Simon
people.about: Owner of a dovecote who gave its produce to Rav Yehuda

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: The recipient, who asks Shmuel how to take possession

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: The Sage who tells Rav Yehuda to bang on the nest

terms.meaning: A structure where pigeons nest.

terms.term: acquisition by means of a cloth
terms.meaning: A formal way of transferring ownership: one party hands the other a cloth, and with it the deal becomes binding.
A Jewish holiday on which, as on the Sabbath, much work is forbidden; the Gemara considers whether the question was about preparing birds to slaughter on it.

10.note: A father told his son to climb to the top of a building and bring him fledglings. The son climbed up, sent away the mother bird and took the young, and on the way back down he fell and died. Rabbi Ya'akov asks where this son's long life and well-being went, since the Torah promises them for both of these commandments, and concludes that "that your days may be long" refers to the world that is entirely long, and "that it may go well with you" to the world where all is good.
10.why: Rabbi Ya'akov has just taught that every reward the Torah states for a commandment is paid in the World-to-Come; this case is his proof, and the Gemara goes on to test it by asking whether it really happened and whether the son was being punished for sinful thoughts.

terms.meaning: One of the Ten Commandments; like sending away the mother bird, the Torah promises long days for keeping it.
The Torah commandment that one who finds a nest must send away the mother before taking the young, with a promise of well-being and long life.

terms.term: the world that is entirely long
terms.meaning: Rabbi Ya'akov's reading of the promised long life as referring to the World-to-Come, the life after this one.

11.note: Rav Mari bar Rahel had a flock of animals. He would transfer ownership of the ears of the unborn firstborn to a gentile, which removed their firstborn status, yet he still forbade shearing them or working them and gave them to the priests, as if they were ordinary firstborns. In the end, the animals of Rav Mari bar Rahel died.
11.why: The Gemara has just told of Rava ruling that no one follows Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that an animal partly owned by a gentile still has firstborn status; Rav Mari's case uses that exemption, and the Gemara then asks why his animals died.

people.name: Rav Mari bar Rahel
people.about: A Sage who sold the ears of his firstborn animals to a gentile, and whose animals died

terms.meaning: The first male born to a kosher cow, sheep or goat is holy by Torah law: it may not be sheared or worked, and is given to a priest.
Selling even a small part of an unborn animal to a gentile makes it jointly owned, which exempts it from firstborn status.
A non-Jew.

12.note: Kontrokos, a government officer, put two questions to Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai. First: the Levite families add up to 22,300, yet the tribe's total is given as 22,000, so where did 300 go? Rabban Yohanan answered that those 300 were themselves firstborns, and a firstborn cannot redeem another firstborn. Then: Moses collected 201 talents and 11 maneh of silver, but the text records giving only 100 talents. Was Moses a thief, a gambler, or bad at arithmetic? Rabban Yohanan answered that Moses was a trustworthy treasurer and expert in accounts, but the Sanctuary's maneh was double the ordinary one.
12.why: The Gemara has been discussing the firstborn in the wilderness and how the Levites took their place; this exchange explains why 300 Levites could not count toward that exchange, and the Gemara then examines where the doubled maneh comes from.

people.name: Kontrokos
people.about: A government officer who challenges the Torah's numbers

people.name: Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai
people.about: The Sage who answers both of Kontrokos's challenges

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Sage who explains why a firstborn Levite cannot redeem an Israelite firstborn

people.name: Moses
people.about: Leader who collected and gave the Tabernacle silver; Kontrokos accuses him and Rabban Yohanan defends him

terms.meaning: Members of the tribe of Levi, who took the place of the Israelite firstborn in sacred service; each Levite redeemed one firstborn.
Units of silver weight. Here a talent is 60 maneh, and an ordinary maneh is 25 shekels.
The portable sanctuary the Israelites built in the wilderness, funded partly by a half-shekel from every man.

13.note: Shimon HaAmasoni used to draw a new teaching from every occurrence of the small Hebrew word "et" in the Torah. When he reached "You shall fear the Lord your God," which also has "et," he gave the method up, since nothing could be added to the fear of God. His students asked what would become of all the "et"s he had already interpreted. He answered that just as he was rewarded for interpreting them, he would be rewarded for withdrawing. The verse stayed unexplained until Rabbi Akiva came and taught that its "et" includes Torah scholars, who must also be feared.
13.why: The Gemara has just said that Rabbi Shimon derives the ban on camel's milk from the word "et," while the Rabbis do not interpret "et" at all; this teaching is cited to show where the Rabbis' refusal comes from.

people.name: Shimon HaAmasoni
people.about: A Sage who interpreted every "et" in the Torah, then withdrew from the method

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: The Sage who later explained the "et" in the verse about fearing God

terms.meaning: A small Hebrew word marking the object of a verb, with no meaning of its own in translation; some Sages read it as hinting at something extra.
A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core collection of Jewish law.

14.note: The Roman emperor asked Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya how long a snake is pregnant. He said seven years; the emperor objected that the sages of Athens had bred snakes that gave birth in three. Rabbi Yehoshua said the Jews were wiser, and the emperor dared him to defeat the sixty Athenian sages and bring them back. Sailing to Athens, he tricked a butcher into showing him their hidden school, used reversed sandal prints to get its guards killed, and beat the sages at riddles: a house in the air, a field of knives, eggs of a black hen. Lodged in his ship, they were carried to the emperor. Soil from Athens restored their arrogance, the emperor let Rabbi Yehoshua do as he wished, and they were defeated by a jug that swallowed water until their shoulders gave out.
14.why: The Gemara has been working out snakes' gestation from the curse on the snake in Genesis, reaching seven years; the story opens with that same figure, which Rabbi Yehoshua defends before the emperor.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya
people.about: The Jewish Sage who answers the emperor and outwits the sages of Athens

people.name: the emperor
people.about: The Roman ruler who questions Rabbi Yehoshua and sends him to Athens

people.name: the sages of Athens
people.about: Sixty wise men in a guarded school whom Rabbi Yehoshua defeats in a contest of riddles

terms.meaning: A place in the sea where, the text says, the water swallows everything near it; water taken from there will not fill a vessel.
A sacred name of God which, in Talmudic stories, a Sage can say aloud to work wonders, as Rabbi Yehoshua does to float in the air.

15.note: Rav Nahman, Rav Amram and Rami bar Hama were travelling on a ferry. While Rav Amram stepped away to relieve himself, a woman came and asked the other two whether someone made impure by a corpse may immerse in a ritual bath and then eat teruma grown outside the Land of Israel. Rav Nahman said to Rami bar Hama: do we even have the sprinkling of the red heifer's ashes? Rami bar Hama suggested they wait for the old man, Rav Amram. Meanwhile Rav Amram returned and said that Rav taught: such a person may immerse and eat teruma from outside the Land.
15.why: Shmuel has just ruled that teruma from outside the Land of Israel is forbidden only to someone whose impurity comes from his own body, not to one who touched a corpse; the ferry question tests that, and the Gemara afterward rules that the law does not follow Rav Amram's report.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: One of three Sages on the ferry; he doubts that immersion can help without the red heifer

people.name: Rav Amram
people.about: The older Sage of the three, who returns and reports Rav's ruling

people.name: Rami bar Hama
people.about: Sage on the ferry who suggests waiting for Rav Amram

people.name: Rav
people.about: Sage whose ruling Rav Amram quotes

terms.meaning: A portion of produce given to priests, which must be eaten only in a state of ritual purity.

terms.term: impure through contact with a corpse
terms.meaning: The most severe kind of ritual impurity, which by Torah law is removed only by sprinkling with water mixed with the ashes of a red heifer.

terms.term: sprinkling of the ashes of the red heifer
terms.meaning: The purification rite for corpse impurity, which could no longer be performed in the Sages' time.
A pool of natural water (mikveh) in which a person immerses to become ritually pure.

16.note: A certain butcher was suspected of selling the forbidden fat of the kidney near the thigh as the permitted fat of the intestines. Rava penalized him by forbidding him to sell even nuts. Rav Pappa challenged Rava: whose opinion was he following? If Rabbi Yehuda's, he should have forbidden the butcher to sell even water and salt. Rava's reply is not part of this story.
16.why: The mishna has just recorded Rabbi Yehuda's view that a man suspected about teruma may not sell even water and salt, against Rabbi Shimon's view that only related items are barred; Rava's penalty is tested against that dispute.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who penalizes the suspected butcher

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: Sage who questions which opinion Rava's penalty follows

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: Sage of the mishna who forbids buying even water and salt from a suspect

terms.term: fat of the kidney adjacent to the thigh
terms.meaning: A kind of animal fat that Jewish law forbids eating, unlike the permitted fat around the intestines.

16.flag: The story stops at Rav Pappa's challenge; Rava's answer, which explains why he banned nuts, is in the next segment and is left out.

17.note: Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei were unsure about a question of ritual purity, and the Sages sent students to ask the son of Rabbi Hanina ben Antigonus to look into it. They found him carrying ritually pure items; he seated Sages from his own school beside the students, not trusting the students with his pure items, and stood to examine the question. The students reported this to Rabbi Yehuda, who said angrily that this man's father degraded Torah scholars and the son does too. Rabbi Yosei answered: let the elder's honor stay in its place. Since the Temple was destroyed, priests have held themselves to a higher standard and do not hand pure items to anyone.
17.why: A teaching has just required even a Torah scholar to commit, before three members, to the purity rules of a haver; Rabbi Yohanan dates that rule to this incident, when scholars were not trusted with pure items.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: Sage who says when the ruling about Torah scholars was taught

people.name: the son of Rabbi Hanina ben Antigonus
people.about: A priest who does not trust the visiting students with his ritually pure items

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: Sage who is unsure of the purity question and is angered by the treatment of the students

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: Sage who defends the priest's conduct

people.name: Rabbi Hanina ben Antigonus
people.about: The priest's father, whom Rabbi Yehuda accuses of degrading Torah scholars

terms.meaning: Food or objects kept in a state of ritual purity, which can be made impure by contact with someone who is not careful about purity rules.
Literally 'associate': a person who has formally committed to keep strict rules of ritual purity and tithing.

18.note: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar told, in Rabbi Meir's name, of a woman who was married to a haver, a man strict about purity laws, and used to tie his phylacteries onto his hand. She later married a tax collector and tied tax seals onto his hand instead. The incident shows how strongly a husband shapes his wife's piety.
18.why: A teaching has just said that the wife of a haver who marries an ordinary man need not commit anew to haver practices; Rabbi Meir disagrees, and this incident is his illustration. The discussion then turns to whether those who abandon haver status can be taken back.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: Sage who holds that even a haver's former wife must commit anew to haver practices

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
people.about: Sage who tells the incident in Rabbi Meir's name

terms.meaning: Literally 'associate': a person who has formally committed to keep strict rules of ritual purity and tithing.
Tefillin: small leather boxes holding Torah verses, bound with straps on the arm and head during prayer.
In the Sages' world, a tax collector was seen as untrustworthy, often taking more than was owed.
Marks or tags tied on to show that tax had been paid.

18.flag: Only the first segment is a story (the woman who married a haver and then a tax collector); the rest are legal opinions on whether haverim who retract are taken back.

19.note: The Sages once needed Rav Huna bar Hiyya for some matter, and Rabba, Rav Yosef and four hundred pairs of Sages went up to his home; hearing they were coming, he set out four hundred chairs for them. Later they heard he had become a tax collector and sent word: go to your important post, and to your former status. He replied that he had repented and was no longer a tax collector. Rav Yosef did not go to him, but Rabba did. Rav Yosef cited a teaching that one who leaves tax collecting is not accepted back; Rabba cited its later version, that such a man is like anyone else.
19.why: A teaching has just recorded that the Sages first barred a haver who became a tax collector even after he quit, and later changed their minds; Rav Yosef and Rabba each act on one stage of that teaching.

people.name: Rav Huna bar Hiyya
people.about: A man the Sages needed, who became a tax collector and later said he had repented

people.name: Rabba
people.about: Sage who goes to Rav Huna bar Hiyya after he repents

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: Sage who refuses to go, holding that a former tax collector is not taken back

terms.meaning: In the Sages' world, a tax collector was seen as untrustworthy, so a haver who took the job lost his standing.
A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core collection of Jewish law.

20.note: Rav Sheshet was troubled at night by a contradiction about selling animal tithe meat, and by morning he resolved it from a baraita: the mishna speaks of tithe animals owned by young orphans, who were allowed to sell so as not to suffer a loss. His attendant, Rav Idi, heard the explanation and repeated it in the study hall without saying it was Rav Sheshet's. Rav Sheshet heard and was annoyed, saying: the one who stung me, let a scorpion sting him. The Gemara asks why it mattered to him, and begins to answer with Rav's reading of the verse "I will dwell in Your tent forever."
20.why: The Gemara has just set the mishna, which lets animal tithe meat be sold in the owner's house, against a baraita that forbids selling it at all; Rav Sheshet's resolution answers that, and the story then turns to why a teaching should be cited in its author's name.

people.name: Rav Sheshet
people.about: Sage who resolves the difficulty and is annoyed when it is repeated without his name

people.name: Rav Idi
people.about: Rav Sheshet's attendant, who repeats the teaching in the study hall without credit

people.name: Rav
people.about: Sage whose reading of a psalm explains why being quoted matters

terms.meaning: Every tenth animal born in a herd is holy and brought as an offering; its meat normally may not be sold.
The duty to prevent another person's loss, used here to allow orphans to sell meat they could not finish.
A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core collection of Jewish law.

20.flag: The story stops mid-explanation: Rav's question about the psalm is included, but his answer (that a scholar wants his teachings said in his name after death) is in the next segment.
